title: The Alchemist’s Recipe — Introduction to Algorithms

learningObjectives.description: Explain an algorithm as a finite, clear plan for a goal.
Explain why dependent steps need the right order.
Recognize a repeated pattern of instructions.
Trace both outcomes of a simple IF/ELSE decision.
Use a bounded loop to repeat a group the right number of times.
Remove unnecessary steps while preserving the intended result.

variants.intro: Hexi: Help me brew my first pretend potion! Pick a recipe, follow a color clue, and find a repeating pattern. No real ingredients or code needed.

sections.title: A recipe with a goal
paragraphs: An algorithm is a clear plan. It has steps and an ending. Hexi’s goal is a pretend glowing potion.

sections.title: Keep the needed order
paragraphs: You already know how to put steps in order. Now choose only the steps our recipe needs. Add pretend water before stirring.

sections.title: Spot a repeating group
paragraphs: Moon, leaf. Moon, leaf. The small group is moon then leaf. Look for the same group again.

sections.title: A choice with two paths
paragraphs: IF the pretend potion is blue, add a star. ELSE add a leaf. Choose one path, not both.

sections.title: Repeat a whole group
paragraphs: Repeat means do the same group again. Repeat “moon, leaf” three times makes six pretend ingredients. Stop after three groups.

sections.title: Fewer steps, same result
paragraphs: Our recipe needs water, stirring, and serving. A dance in the middle changes nothing in this story. Leave it out. Real recipes can have important safety steps: never skip those.

choices.text: A clear plan that reaches a goal and stops
choices.feedback: Hexi: Exactly! A plan needs clear actions, an intended result, and an ending.

questions.prompt: IF blue THEN star, ELSE leaf. What happens for green?

choices.text: Add both a star and a leaf
choices.feedback: Hexi: Try again. Green is not blue, so follow ELSE only.
Hexi: Exactly! Green is not blue, so follow ELSE only.
Hexi: Try again. Green is not blue, so follow ELSE only.

questions.prompt: Repeat moon then leaf three times. How many ingredients are added?

choices.feedback: Hexi: Try again. Each group has two ingredients: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
Hexi: Try again. Each group has two ingredients: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.
Hexi: Exactly! Each group has two ingredients: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6.

variants.intro: Hexi: Build on sequencing by tracing decisions, identifying repeated groups, and improving a plan without changing its goal.

sections.title: A recipe with a goal
paragraphs: An algorithm is a finite sequence of precise instructions for a goal. Inputs describe the starting state; outputs describe the intended result. We will trace supplied plans rather than execute them.
sections.pseudocode:
INPUT: water and ingredients
OUTPUT: a served pretend potion

sections.title: Keep the needed order
paragraphs: The earlier sequencing lesson introduced order and debugging. Now remove a redundant operation while keeping dependencies: water, stir, then serve the pretend potion.

sections.title: Spot a repeating group
paragraphs: A repeated pattern is a group in the same order: moon → leaf, then moon → leaf again. The group is two instructions, not one ingredient.
sections.pseudocode: MOON, LEAF | MOON, LEAF | MOON, LEAF

sections.title: A choice with two paths
paragraphs: IF tests a condition. If it is true, follow the first path; ELSE follow the other. Trace blue and non-blue inputs so you do not accidentally apply both branches.
sections.pseudocode:
IF color = blue THEN star
ELSE leaf

sections.title: Repeat a whole group
paragraphs: A bounded loop repeats its whole body a specified number of times, then stops. Three iterations of a two-item group yield six items. A loop is not automatically an infinite loop.
sections.pseudocode:
REPEAT 3 TIMES:
  add moon
  add leaf

sections.title: Fewer steps, same result
paragraphs: An unnecessary step can be removed only if the intended result still holds. In this fictional recipe a decorative pause does not change the potion. A loop can reduce copied instructions without reducing the work performed.
sections.pseudocode:
KEEP required operations
REMOVE only the stated redundant step

sections.title: A recipe with a goal
paragraphs: An algorithm describes clear, finite steps that transform an input into an expected output. Example: an unpacked parcel and label become a correctly addressed, sealed parcel.
sections.pseudocode:
INPUT: unpacked parcel
OUTPUT: sealed, labeled parcel

sections.title: Keep the needed order
paragraphs: Thinking Like a Programmer introduced sequencing. Here we also preserve dependencies while selecting only necessary operations: pack before sealing, seal before labeling in our stated workflow.

sections.title: Spot a repeating group
paragraphs: Printing labels A then B repeatedly contains the unit A → B. Identify the whole repeated unit before replacing copied instructions with a loop.
sections.pseudocode: A, B | A, B | A, B

sections.title: A choice with two paths
paragraphs: A condition selects exactly one branch. IF a parcel is marked urgent, choose express; ELSE choose standard. Test both a true and a false condition.
sections.pseudocode:
IF urgent THEN express
ELSE standard

sections.title: Repeat a whole group
paragraphs: REPEAT 3 TIMES means three iterations of the entire body, then stop. A two-label body repeated three times produces six labels, not three.
sections.pseudocode:
REPEAT 3 TIMES:
  print A
  print B

sections.title: Fewer steps, same result
paragraphs: Removing a second identical status lookup is useful only under the stated unchanged-input assumption. Fewer written instructions do not automatically mean less runtime work: loops can shorten a plan while doing the same operations. Never remove validation or safety checks just because they look repetitive.
sections.pseudocode:
LOOK UP unchanged status once
DISPLAY status

practiceTasks.title: Build a smaller recipe
practiceTasks.instruction: Choose three needed steps in order. Leave out the dance pause. These are story ingredients, not a real potion recipe.
practiceTasks.goal: Water first. Stir next. Serve last. The dance does not change our story potion.
practiceTasks.input: Four supplied operations; three are required.
practiceTasks.explanation: Water, stir, serve! You kept the needed steps and left out the dance.
practiceTasks.hint: Leave out the dance. Add water before stirring, then serve.

slots.label: Step 1
slots.hint: Water goes in first.

slots.label: Step 2
slots.hint: Stir after adding water.

slots.label: Step 3
slots.hint: Serve after stirring.

practiceTasks.title: Follow both paths
practiceTasks.instruction: IF the potion is blue, add a star; ELSE add a leaf. Trace each input separately.
practiceTasks.goal: Choose exactly one branch for each input.
practiceTasks.explanation: The first input makes the condition true. The second makes it false, so only the ELSE action applies.
practiceTasks.hint: Check the condition for each input. ELSE is used only when the IF condition is false.

slots.label: Blue potion
slots.hint: Read this input again: choose the true branch or the ELSE branch, never both.

slots.label: Green potion
slots.hint: Read this input again: choose the true branch or the ELSE branch, never both.

practiceTasks.title: Find the repeat recipe
practiceTasks.instruction: Target: moon leaf moon leaf moon leaf. Choose the smallest shown repeating group, how often it repeats, and its final output.
practiceTasks.goal: Reproduce the target exactly, then stop.
practiceTasks.input: moon leaf moon leaf moon leaf
practiceTasks.expectedOutput: moon leaf moon leaf moon leaf
practiceTasks.explanation: The two-item group repeats three times. The output contains six items in alternating order. A loop shortens the written plan but still adds all six items.
practiceTasks.hint: Mark off each pair. There are three pairs, with two items in each pair.

slots.label: Repeating group
slots.hint: Keep both items in the target’s order.

slots.label: Number of repeats
slots.hint: Count the pairs, not the individual items.

slots.label: Final output

options.text: moon leaf moon leaf moon leaf

slots.hint: Three two-item groups produce six items.
